title: Everyday wording vs formal wording
text: Choose wording for the audience and purpose. A formal alternative can change tone without being more accurate. Preserve the original claim, certainty, and politeness; a grammatical informal sentence is not automatically wrong.
when_to_use: Choose this for a local word-level register change. Use the sentence or phrase note when restructuring the whole utterance.

examples.text: Please [get] written consent. -> Please obtain written consent.
Could you [help] with the survey? -> Could you assist with the survey?
We will [ask for] permission. -> We will request permission.
We need to [get] approval first. -> We need to obtain approval first.

Do not frame this as a tense or agreement error when the issue is register.
selection_rationale: Retained to distinguish everyday wording vs formal wording in the existing drill curriculum. Choose this for a local word-level register change. Use the sentence or phrase note when restructuring the whole utterance.
reference_scope: Register depends on context and grammatical/lexical choices. Task-specific examples and boundaries are original editorial material, not claims of source endorsement.

counterexamples.text: Original: We might finish today. Bad rewrite: We will finish today. The rewrite removes uncertainty.
counterexamples.reason: Keep the modal might; the source does not promise completion.

title: General wording vs precise synonym
text: A replacement must fit the word sense, grammar, and surrounding words. Similar dictionary meanings do not guarantee interchangeability. A longer alternative such as utilize is not inherently more precise than use.
when_to_use: Use for a contextual word substitution without a special grammatical transformation; check the whole sentence after inserting the answer.

examples.text: The diagram [shows] the process. -> The diagram illustrates the process.
Please [look at closely] the signature. -> Please examine the signature.
The meeting will [start] at noon. -> The meeting will begin at noon.
The project was very [big]. -> The project was very substantial.

title: Loose phrase vs single precise verb
text: Replace a phrase with one verb only when it expresses the same action and takes compatible objects and prepositions. Preserve tense and agent. Concision does not license inventing successful outcomes.
when_to_use: Use when a card explicitly requests a single verb, before applying generic synonym or register guidance.

She [made improvements to] the draft. -> She improved the draft.
We [gave an explanation of] the rule. -> We explained the rule.
He [talked about] the risks at length. -> He addressed the risks at length.

title: Active voice vs passive voice
text: For an ordinary transitive clause, passive be plus a past participle makes the object the subject. Preserve tense, participants, and negation. Choose voice for focus; the passive agent may be omitted when unknown or unneeded, but do not invent an agent when converting back.
when_to_use: Use for an explicit active/passive transformation, not a general demand to sound formal.

examples.text: Mira checked the invoice. -> The invoice was checked by Mira.
The parcel was packed by Leo. -> Leo packed the parcel.
They have not approved the plan. -> The plan has not been approved by them.
The committee reviewed the proposal. -> The proposal was reviewed by the committee.

title: Two clauses vs participle clause
text: An introductory participle clause normally shares its understood subject with the main clause. Having plus a past participle marks an earlier completed action; an -ing clause may describe simultaneous activity. Check subject and time relations before combining sentences.
when_to_use: Use when combining clauses with a participle opener. Do not use for noun-identifying relative clauses.

examples.text: Nora checked the address. Then she mailed the form. -> Having checked the address, Nora mailed the form.
Omar walked home. He listened to a podcast as he walked. -> Walking home, Omar listened to a podcast.
The students finished the task. Then they left. -> Having finished the task, the students left.
She studied the data. She reached a conclusion. -> Having studied the data, she reached a conclusion.

Bad: Walking to the office, the rain soaked me. The grammatical subject would be the rain, not the walker.
selection_rationale: Retained to distinguish two clauses vs participle clause in the existing drill curriculum. Use when combining clauses with a participle opener. Do not use for noun-identifying relative clauses.
reference_scope: Shared-subject participle constructions and earlier completed actions. Task-specific examples and boundaries are original editorial material, not claims of source endorsement.

counterexamples.text: Bad: Walking to the office, the rain soaked me. The grammatical subject would be the rain, not the walker.
counterexamples.reason: The introductory clause needs the walker as the main clause subject.

title: Two sentences vs relative clause
text: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing is intended. It normally has no surrounding commas. Use who for people and which or that for things; preserve the noun reference. Choosing defining rather than non-defining changes the information structure.
when_to_use: Use when extra information selects one referent from several, or the card explicitly requests a defining relative clause.

examples.text: Several analysts applied. The analyst who speaks Arabic was selected. -> The selected analyst is identified by the clause who speaks Arabic.
Choose the file. It contains the final figures. -> Choose the file that contains the final figures.
I need the tool. It opens this panel. -> I need the tool that opens this panel.
The manager approved the budget. She leads the project. -> The manager who leads the project approved the budget.

If there is only one already identified sister, adding identifying information without commas may imply a different context.

title: Casual sentence vs formal rewrite
text: Rewrite the sentence in a neutral professional tone while keeping its propositions intact. Do not add evidence, deadlines, magnitude, or completed actions. Formality does not require passive voice or abstract nouns.

title: Two sentences vs non-restrictive relative clause
text: A non-defining relative clause adds parenthetical information about an already identified referent. Separate an inserted clause with two commas and keep a relative pronoun such as who or which; do not use that. Contrast this with a defining clause that selects a referent.
when_to_use: Use when extra information is parenthetical, not necessary to identify the noun.

examples.text: Asha lives in Leeds. She designed this logo. -> Asha, who designed this logo, lives in Leeds.
This single invoice is overdue. It arrived on Friday. -> This invoice, which arrived on Friday, is overdue.
Our only office has reopened. It closed in May. -> Our only office, which closed in May, has reopened.

title: Casual conditional vs formal inverted conditional
text: Conditional inversion can replace if with should, were, or had. Keep the condition type and time reference: should plus base verb, were to for a hypothetical action, and had plus past participle for a past counterfactual. Inversion changes register and can affect perceived likelihood.

title: Verb phrase vs nominalized form
text: Nominalization expresses an action through a noun, such as approval or revision. It can help discuss a process as a topic, but often adds words or hides the actor. Preserve the actor when it matters; a noun-based version is not automatically better writing.
